explanations.answer: Calls four kings to help him attack Gibeon
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, sends word to four other kings: Hoham king of Hebron, Piram king of Jarmuth, Japhia king of Lachish, and Debir king of Eglon. His message says, “Come up and help me. We will attack Gibeon…” (Joshua 10:4). He's alarmed, so he does what you do when the group chat is the only plan you've got. Four messages go out, and he's not doing this one alone.

explanations.answer: Sends gifts to make peace with Joshua
explanations.explanation: Nope, no gift basket in this one. Adoni-zedek is the king of Jerusalem, and the text never has him reach out to Joshua, Israel's leader. The ones who made peace with Israel were the people of Gibeon, and that's exactly what bothers Adoni-zedek. His message goes to four other kings, and he asks them to help him attack Gibeon (Joshua 10:3-4).

explanations.answer: Moves all his people out of Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: I get it, alarmed people sometimes head for the exits. But the text never says he moves his people out of Jerusalem. It says he sends word to four kings and asks them to come up and help him attack Gibeon (Joshua 10:3-4). Then the five kings join forces, advance with all their armies and camp before Gibeon (Joshua 10:5). Adoni-zedek isn't running from this problem, he's recruiting for it.

explanations.answer: Joshua in the camp at Gilgal
explanations.explanation: Right on target, friend. The men of Gibeon send word to Joshua, Israel's leader, in the camp at Gilgal. They say, “Do not abandon your servants. Come quickly and save us!” (Joshua 10:6). That's a message with no small talk in it.

explanations.answer: Pharaoh king of Egypt
explanations.explanation: Pharaoh, Egypt's king, never shows up anywhere in this passage. The men of Gibeon send word to Joshua in the camp at Gilgal. They say, “Do not abandon your servants. Come quickly and save us!” (Joshua 10:6). When you need help fast, you call the one name on your list, and Gibeon's list says Joshua.

explanations.answer: Hiram king of Tyre
explanations.explanation: Hiram, king of Tyre, isn't in this story at all. The men of Gibeon send word to Joshua, Israel's leader, in the camp at Gilgal. They beg him not to abandon them and to come quickly, because all the kings of the Amorites from the hill country have joined forces against them (Joshua 10:6). It's a short list of people to call, and Joshua is the one on it.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: True, baker. Verse 7 says Joshua and his whole army, including all the mighty men of valor, came from Gilgal. Not a small team and not a few volunteers. When Gibeon calls, the whole army moves, and I think that's one loud parade of sandals.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: This one is true, friend. The text says Joshua and his whole army, including all the mighty men of valor, came from Gilgal (Joshua 10:7). So Joshua doesn't send a small group or stay behind. He comes out with everybody.

explanations.answer: Don't be afraid because I've handed them over to you
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The LORD tells Joshua, “Do not be afraid of them, for I have delivered them into your hand. Not one of them shall stand against you.” (Joshua 10:8). Five armies are waiting, and the LORD speaks straight to the fear first.

explanations.answer: Send messengers to the five kings and talk first
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd think of talking first, but that's not what the LORD says here. He tells Joshua, “Do not be afraid of them, for I have delivered them into your hand.” (Joshua 10:8). There's no mention of messengers or a meeting. The LORD's word is about the five kings being delivered into Joshua's hand.

explanations.answer: Take only your mighty men and leave the rest behind
explanations.explanation: Close, because the mighty men are in the story. But verse 7 says Joshua came with his whole army, including all the mighty men of valor. And the LORD's words in verse 8 aren't about who to bring at all. He says, “Do not be afraid of them…” (Joshua 10:8).

explanations.answer: confusion
explanations.explanation: Yes, confusion. Verse 10 says the LORD threw them into confusion before Israel. Joshua had marched all night and caught them by surprise, and then the LORD stepped in too. I think those armies had no idea what hit them.

explanations.answer: darkness
explanations.explanation: I see where darkness might come from, since Joshua marched all night to get there. But the text never says the LORD threw them into darkness. It says He threw them into confusion before Israel (Joshua 10:10). Later in the day, the sun actually stands still over Gibeon (Joshua 10:12-13), so the story is heading toward more light, not less.

explanations.answer: chains
explanations.explanation: Chains would be a neat way to stop an army, but I don't see any in this story. Verse 10 says the LORD threw them into confusion before Israel (Joshua 10:10). No rope, no locks, just an army that suddenly can't get its act together. I've had mornings like that with a bowl of dough and no recipe, but never with a whole army!

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: This one comes out the other way. The text says more of them were killed by the hailstones than by the swords of the Israelites (Joshua 10:11). I think this part of the story is a heavy one. The LORD cast the large hailstones down from the sky as they fled.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: False is right. Verse 11 says the LORD cast down large hailstones from the sky, and more of them were killed by the hailstones than by the swords of the Israelites. I think this part is heavy, so I'll just say it plainly. The hailstones came from the LORD, and the text puts them ahead of the swords.

explanations.answer: The sun and moon to stand still
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Joshua speaks to the LORD in front of all Israel and says, “O sun, stand still over Gibeon, O moon, over the Valley of Aijalon.” (Joshua 10:12). That's a big thing to ask out loud with everybody watching. Then the text says the sun stood still and the moon stopped (Joshua 10:13).

explanations.answer: The stars to fall on the enemy
explanations.explanation: Stars falling would make a dramatic story, but Joshua never mentions them. He speaks to the LORD about the sun and the moon. He says, “O sun, stand still over Gibeon, O moon, over the Valley of Aijalon.” (Joshua 10:12). My own sky has plenty of stars from my cookie boxes, and none of them were asked to fall.

explanations.answer: Dark clouds to hide the whole army
explanations.explanation: Hiding the army would be a different request altogether. Joshua says, “O sun, stand still over Gibeon, O moon, over the Valley of Aijalon.” (Joshua 10:12). He calls for the sun and the moon to hold still, not for clouds. And verse 13 tells us the sun did stand still.

explanations.answer: The LORD listened to the voice of a man
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The writer says, “There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD listened to the voice of a man, because the LORD fought for Israel.” (Joshua 10:14). The man is Joshua, who had just spoken to the LORD about the sun and moon. The writer says the LORD listened.

explanations.answer: The LORD sent His angel before the camp
explanations.explanation: An angel going before the camp does show up elsewhere in the Bible, like in Exodus 14:19, but not in this passage. Verse 14 says what makes the day one of a kind: the LORD listened to the voice of a man. That man is Joshua, who had just called out to the sun and moon. The writer adds that the LORD fought for Israel.

explanations.answer: The LORD spoke aloud to the whole army
explanations.explanation: In this passage the LORD speaks to Joshua. He says, “Do not be afraid of them…” (Joshua 10:8). The thing that makes this day one of a kind goes the other direction. Verse 14 says the LORD listened to the voice of a man, and that man is Joshua, who had spoken to the LORD in front of Israel.
